claims.source: The strong attractiveness of digging sites for termite aggregation means that in all these studies digging and deposition actions mostly come in pairs, which prevents us from identifying the genuine cues for pellet collection and deposition (Bardunias and Su, 2009b; Bardunias and Su, 2010; Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies: Bardunias and Su, 2009b; Bardunias and Su, 2010; Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In Calovi et al., 2019, termites preferentially aggregate in concave regions of a surface and rearrange nest material at those locations.
claims.source: For example, in Calovi et al., 2019 termites are shown to preferentially aggregate in concave regions of a surface and they would simply rearrange nest material (both digging and building) at those locations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Calovi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition.
claims.source: Even if digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition (Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017), and for this reason digging and construction often co-localize in space, it is clear that building and digging cannot completely overlap, or the two activities would simply cancel one the effect of the other: termites must be able to differentiate between the sites of these contrasting activities through digging- or building-specific cues.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fouquet et al., 2014 and Green et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Termites must be able to differentiate between digging and building sites through specific cues.
claims.source: Even if digging sites provide a template for pellet deposition (Fouquet et al., 2014; Green et al., 2017), and for this reason digging and construction often co-localize in space, it is clear that building and digging cannot completely overlap, or the two activities would simply cancel one the effect of the other: termites must be able to differentiate between the sites of these contrasting activities through digging- or building-specific cues.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that digging and building cannot completely overlap.

claims.claim: The model proposed in Ocko et al., 2019 indicates that a generic 'colony odor' undergoing advection and diffusion within the nest could provide a sufficient cue for determining the overall mound shape.
claims.source: For example, the model proposed in Ocko et al., 2019 indicates that a generic 'colony odor' undergoing advection and diffusion within the nest could provide a sufficient cue for determining the overall mound shape, so leaving a possible role of a construction pheromone only for the structuring of small scale nest features such as pillars and walls.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ocko et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Facchini et al., 2020 proposed a model in which small scale nest features can be produced in the absence of a construction pheromone by assuming that termites respond to the local curvature of emerging nest features.
claims.source: Facchini et al., 2020 further proposed a model in which also small scale nest features can be produced in the absence of a construction pheromone, by assuming that termites respond to the local curvature of these emerging nest features.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Facchini et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The building rules implemented in previous computational models are not empirically validated from direct observations of termite worker building behavior.
claims.source: While these models reproduce a number of structures observed in real termite nests, the building rules implemented in the models are not empirically validated from direct observations of the building behavior of termite workers.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the state of validation for computational models.

claims.claim: Pellet collection activity was distributed homogeneously all over the clay disk in the experiments.
claims.source: Pellet collection activity was distributed homogeneously all over the clay disk that we provided at the center of the experimental arena.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Deposition activity was concentrated at the tips of pre-existing pillars and along the edges of the clay disk.
claims.source: Conversely, deposition activity was concentrated at the tips of pre-existing pillars, and along the edges of the clay disk itself.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: Termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets.
claims.source: Thus, termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets while they target specific regions when depositing, which suggests that those regions must express a strong stimulus for deposition.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing homogeneous collection distribution.

claims.claim: Termites target specific regions when depositing pellets.
claims.source: Thus, termites do not show a preference for where they collect pellets while they target specific regions when depositing, which suggests that those regions must express a strong stimulus for deposition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing concentrated deposition patterns.

claims.claim: Occupancy is high close to the pillars and to the Petri dish walls in the experimental setup.
claims.source: Occupancy is high close to the pillars and to the Petri dish walls, has intermediate values within the clay disk, and drops at the top of the pillars and right outside of the clay disk (i.e. precisely where deposits are recorded).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The top edge of the wall attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips in 7 out of 11 experiments.
claims.source: We report that the top edge attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips pointing to curvature, rather than elevation, as the dominant cue in 7 out of 11 experiments (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claims.claim: Curvature, rather than elevation, is the dominant cue for pellet deposition.
claims.source: We report that the top edge attracted many deposits, but pellet deposition focused at the wall tips pointing to curvature, rather than elevation, as the dominant cue in 7 out of 11 experiments (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that depositions focused at wall tips (high curvature) rather than uniformly along the top edge (constant elevation).

claims.claim: Experiments and simulations show a fair agreement as pellet depositions and initial growth concentrate in the same regions which are those where the surface is the most convex.
claims.source: Experiments and simulations show a fair agreement as pellet depositions and initial growth concentrate in the same regions which are those where the surface is the most convex, as depicted in white in Figure 3C–F.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data with simulation results shown in Figures 2C and 3.

claims.claim: The qualitative agreement between experimental results and curvature-based simulations supports the idea that surface curvature alone is a sufficient cue that could guide termite depositions.
claims.source: The qualitative agreement between experimental results and curvature-based simulations supports the idea that, at least on a first approximation, surface curvature alone is a sufficient cue that could guide termite depositions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between experimental and simulation results.

claims.claim: The clay disk is maintained constantly humid during experiments.
claims.source: Trying to identify this additional building cue, we recall that the clay disk is maintained constantly humid.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claims.claim: The edges of the disk arena mark the limit between a humid region and the surrounding dry periphery.
claims.source: The edges of the disk arena mark then the limit between a humid region and the surrounding dry periphery.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claims.claim: The clay tone remained unchanged during experiments which suggests that moisture is constantly evaporating from the clay disk while being replenished in water from below.
claims.source: Also, the clay tone remained unchanged during experiments which suggests that moisture is constantly evaporating from the clay disk while being replenished in water from below, and that the overall process is stationary.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claims.claim: A net increase in humidity and a net decrease in temperature was observed coming from outside to inside the clay disk which is the footprint of evaporation.
claims.source: We observed a net increase in humidity and a net decrease in temperature coming from outside to inside the clay disk which is the footprint of evaporation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Inside and outside the clay disk, both humidity and temperature remained relatively stable indicating that the system is roughly in a steady state.
claims.source: Inside and outside the clay disk, both quantities remained relatively stable indicating that the system is roughly in a steady state.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Close enough to the evaporating substrate, humidity transport happens by diffusion.
claims.source: Evaporation is a complex process, but close enough to the evaporating substrate, humidity transport happens by diffusion (Langmuir., 1918; Hisatake et al., 1993) and it is hence fully determined by the humidity gradient.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Langmuir., 1918 and Hisatake et al., 1993.

claims.claim: Termites live in a viscous boundary layer where humidity transport is diffusive.
claims.source: In agreement with previous studies (Soar et al., 2019), we can show with scaling arguments that our termites live in such a viscous boundary layer (see Appendix 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by scaling arguments in Appendix 3 and citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In the diffusive regime, the evaporation flux is directly proportional to the surface curvature of the evaporating substrate.
claims.source: In the diffusive regime, the evaporation flux is directly proportional to the surface curvature of the evaporating substrate (see Appendix 2 for a mathematical proof).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical proof in Appendix 2.

claims.claim: Curvature and evaporation are two completely interchangeable stimuli everywhere except at the edge of the clay disk.
claims.source: As such, curvature and evaporation are two completely interchangeable stimuli everywhere except at the edge of the clay disk, where the transition between clay and perspex material corresponds to a strong humidity gradient in spite of weak surface curvature.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the computational analysis of humidity gradients and surface curvature.

claims.claim: Evaporation flux can explain by itself the deposition patterns observed in the experiments.
claims.source: We then propose that evaporation flux can explain by itself the deposition patterns observed in our experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between evaporation patterns and deposition behavior.

claims.claim: The distribution of salt deposits in chemical garden experiments matches very closely the regions of highest building activity by termites.
claims.source: Remarkably the distribution of the salt deposits matches very closely the regions of highest building activity by termites, both being more pronounced at the edge of the clay disk and at the top of topographic cues (pillar and walls).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of chemical garden experiments (Figure 4C and D) with termite building patterns.

claims.claim: Termite deposition probability covaries with the evaporation flux.
claims.source: This result indicates that termite deposition probability covaries with the evaporation flux, which is consistent with our hypothesis of evaporation as the strongest cue for deposition.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the chemical garden experiments showing correlation between salt deposition (evaporation marker) and termite deposition patterns.

claims.claim: Salt traces are less pronounced on the wall than on the pillars in chemical garden experiments.
claims.source: One may notice that salt traces are less pronounced on the wall (Figure 4D) than on the pillars (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the chemical garden experiments shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: The maximum amplitude of the humidity gradient is weaker in the wall case than in the pillar case.
claims.source: This is consistent with the amplitude of the humidity gradient in a stationary diffusive regime as shown in Figure 4B and A respectively: the maximum amplitude of the gradient is weaker in the wall case.
claims.evidence: This is supported by computational simulations shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: The variability in termite construction patterns is larger in the case of wall cues compared to pillar cues.
claims.source: Possibly, this could explain why in the case of wall cues there is a comparatively much larger variability in the patterns of termite construction (see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: When termites are confronted with the 'wall' cue they are likely to start pellet depositions at the wall tips, but initial pellet depositions started at other locations on the top edge do also occur.
claims.source: When termites are confronted with the 'wall' cue they are likely to start pellet depositions at the wall tips, but initial pellet depositions started at other locations on the top edge do also occur.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Initial pellet depositions are preserved and reinforced by positive feed-back mechanisms.
claims.source: Whatever the initial choice, depositions are then preserved and reinforced by positive feed-back mechanisms which can lead to tightly selected deposition patterns also in the case of the 'wall' cue.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that initial deposition patterns persist and grow.

claims.claim: The edge of the clay disk is almost flat for a termite walking across, but it is also a thin cusp of humid material which is strongly evaporating.
claims.source: In fact, the edge of the clay disk is almost flat (weak convexity) for a termite walking across, but it is also a thin cusp (high convexity) of humid material which is strongly evaporating, similarly to what happens at the edge of a liquid drop and causes the formation of well known coffee stains (Deegan et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is explained by analogy to coffee stain formation, supported by citation to Deegan et al., 1997.

claims.claim: By providing loose and unmarked pellets, the study was able to prompt building activity without digging and to quantify collections and depositions as separate actions.
claims.source: Here, by providing loose and unmarked pellets, we were able to prompt building activity without digging and to quantify collections and depositions as separate actions.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claims.claim: All pellets were progressively displaced during the experiments.
claims.source: We observed that all pellets were progressively displaced and that collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
claims.source: We observed that all pellets were progressively displaced and that collections happened in a relatively random fashion.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing homogeneous collection distribution.

claims.claim: Depositions concentrated at specific parts of the experimental arena which are the tips of the topographic cues and the edges of the clay disk.
claims.source: On the contrary, depositions concentrated at specific parts of the experimental arena which are the tips of the topographic cues and the edges of the clay disk.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: The conditional probability of deposition given termite occupancy was high at the tips of topographic cues and edges of the clay disk.
claims.source: The conditional probability of deposition given termite occupancy was high there, indicating that those regions precisely drive termite depositions rather than generically attracting termite aggregation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The alternative use of pillars and walls as topographic cues allowed disentangling the role of elevation and curvature.
claims.source: The alternative use of pillars and walls as topographic cues allowed us to disentangle the role of elevation and curvature and pointed toward curvature as the most attractive stimulus for deposition.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design strategy.

claims.claim: Surface curvature is a powerful morphogenetic organizer for 3D structure formation as it can drive the formation of pillars, walls and convoluted surfaces.
claims.source: Surface curvature is a powerful morphogenetic organizer for 3D structure formation as it can drive the formation of pillars, walls and convoluted surfaces (Facchini et al., 2020), all features that are observed in the nests of various termite species.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Facchini et al., 2020 and general knowledge about termite nest structures.

claims.claim: The study demonstrates a close coupling between surface curvature and the flux of evaporation from a surface.
claims.source: Here, we were able to demonstrate a close coupling between surface curvature and the flux of evaporation from a surface, so providing a link to a possible stimulus sensed directly by termites.
claims.evidence: This is supported by analytical derivations and experimental results shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The findings reconcile previous discordant results pointing alternately to curvature or to humidity as the relevant stimuli.
claims.source: This also allows us to reconcile previous discordant results pointing alternately to curvature (Calovi et al., 2019; Facchini et al., 2020) or to humidity (Soar et al., 2019; Bardunias et al., 2020) as the relevant stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated relationship between curvature and evaporation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Langmuir., 1918 showed that close enough to the surface of a water droplet, evaporation scales as the inverse of the radius (i.e. as the mean curvature) of the droplet.
claims.source: The idea itself of a relation between curvature and evaporation is not new, as already a century ago, Langmuir., 1918 showed that close enough to the surface of a water droplet, evaporation scales as the inverse of the radius (i.e. as the mean curvature) of the droplet see (Appendix 2 for a derivation).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Langmuir., 1918.

claims.claim: Termites are particularly sensitive to the humidity of their environment because their small size and soft cuticle put them in constant danger of desiccation.
claims.source: It is well known that termites are particularly sensitive to the humidity of their environment, because their small size and soft cuticle put them in constant danger of desiccation.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about termite physiology.

claims.claim: Coptotermes termites can only survive in high-humidity environments such as moist wood or soil.
claims.source: Coptotermes termites in particular are wetwood termites that can only survive in high-humidity environments such as moist wood or soil.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about Coptotermes biology.

claims.claim: In laboratory experiments, C. formosanus termites died within a few days when maintained at 72.9% or less relative humidity, but survived well when humidity was 98%.
claims.source: For example, in laboratory experiments Zukowski and Su, 2017, C. formosanus termites died within a few days when maintained at 72.9% or less relative humidity, but survived well when humidity was 98%.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zukowski and Su, 2017.

claims.claim: Coptotermes gestroi were able to discriminate between chambers with different relative humidity and, after 12 hr, almost all termites were in the highest humidity chamber (98%).
claims.source: Coptotermes gestroi were also able to discriminate between chambers with different relative humidity and, after 12 hr, almost all termites were in the highest humidity chamber (98%), leaving the other chambers with 75% or less relative humidity empty (Gautam and Henderson, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gautam and Henderson, 2011.

claims.claim: Given sufficient time, termites can detect a difference of humidity from 75% to 98% over a spatial scale of centimeters.
claims.source: These results (which are similar also to other results testing termite response to chambers with different soil moisture) indicate that –given a sufficient amount of time– termites can detect a difference of humidity from 75% to 98% over a spatial scale of centimeters.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cited experimental results.

claims.claim: Humidity can affect termite behavior in the context of nest building by triggering nest expansion events.
claims.source: Recent field and laboratory experiments have shown that humidity can affect termite behavior also in the context of nest building (Carey et al., 2019), by triggering nest expansion events (Bardunias et al., 2020; Carey et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Carey et al., 2019; Bardunias et al., 2020; Carey et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Soar et al., 2019 showed that moisture flux affects termite building activity in terms of both pellet collection and deposition.
claims.source: Even more interestingly, Soar et al., 2019 showed that moisture flux affects termite building activity (both in terms of pellet collection and deposition).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Moisture variations not only prompt or inhibit termite building activity, but constitute a local blueprint for construction.
claims.source: Our experiments confirm this trend and suggest that moisture variations not only prompt or inhibit termite building activity, but constitute a local blueprint for construction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results of the current study.

claims.claim: The estimated humidity variations correspond to humidity variation of 10 to 100% across a distance not larger than termite body length.
claims.source: As our termites are millimetre size, the estimated lower and upper boundary correspond to humidity variation of 10 to 100% across a distance not larger than their body length.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the estimated humidity gradients and termite body size.

claims.claim: Humidity variations of 10 to 100% across termite body length must be sensed by termites.
claims.source: We then expect that such variations must be sensed by termites, as they are larger than those that Coptotermes gestroi termites were shown to be able to discriminate over much larger spatial scales in the experiments reviewed above.
claims.evidence: This is inferred by comparing calculated humidity gradients with previously reported termite sensory capabilities.

claims.claim: The experiments do not support a role for a putative cement pheromone added by termites to the building material.
claims.source: Our experiments do not support a role for a putative cement pheromone, added by termites to the building material, which would stimulate pellet depositions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing construction on unmarked materials.

claims.claim: Construction occurred reliably on provided building cues even if they only comprised fresh clay and sterilized pellets with no pheromone markings.
claims.source: In fact, construction occurred reliably on our provided building cues, even if they only comprised fresh clay and sterilized pellets with no pheromone markings.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claims.claim: Simulations indicate that qualitatively similar construction results can be obtained without assuming a role for construction pheromone.
claims.source: Our simulations further indicate that qualitatively similar construction results can be obtained without assuming a role for construction pheromone.
claims.evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The influence of a cement pheromone can be excluded, at least during the early choice of the deposition sites.
claims.source: We can hence exclude the influence of a cement pheromone, at least during the early choice of the deposition sites, in agreement with recent experiments by other authors (Fouquet et al., 2014; Petersen et al., 2015; Green et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the current experimental results and citations to other studies.

claims.claim: In the experiments, the building substrate was constantly moist throughout the entire duration of the experiments.
claims.source: We should point to the fact, however, that in our experiments the building substrate was constantly moist throughout the entire duration of the experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claims.claim: Under conditions where moisture may not constantly replenish the porous wall, the evaporation flux is maintained by the humidity that is naturally embedded in recently dropped pellets.
claims.source: We suggest that under these conditions, the evaporation flux is maintained by the humidity that is naturally embedded in recently dropped pellets, which makes the construction process self-sustainable and is consistent with the hypothesis of a viscous boundary layer extending with termite activity (Soar et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about construction in natural conditions, supported by citation to Soar et al., 2019.

claims.claim: It would be very hard to distinguish between a scenario where evaporation is maintained by pellet humidity and one which involves a putative cement pheromone added directly to manipulated pellets by termites.
claims.source: In practice, it would be very hard to distinguish between such a scenario and one which involves a putative cement pheromone added directly to manipulated pellets by termites.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the difficulty of distinguishing between alternative mechanisms.

claims.claim: Pheromones may play a role in termite building behavior by mediating termite aggregation.
claims.source: More generally, while we do not rule out a possible role of pheromones in termite building behavior (mediating for instance termite aggregation), we have shown that pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns that we see in our experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about possible roles of pheromones not tested in the current study.

claims.claim: Pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns observed in the experiments.
claims.source: More generally, while we do not rule out a possible role of pheromones in termite building behavior (mediating for instance termite aggregation), we have shown that pheromones are not necessary to explain the early deposition patterns that we see in our experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and simulations.

claims.claim: Collective nest construction is a dynamic process and the deposition of new pellets by termites constantly changes the shape and the porosity of the evaporating substrate.
claims.source: In this study, we have focused on understanding how termites respond to well-controlled predefined stimuli. However, collective nest construction is a dynamic process and the deposition of new pellets by termites constantly changes the shape and the porosity of the evaporating substrate, potentially affecting nest growth through positive or negative feedback.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the dynamic nature of nest construction.

claims.claim: Termites can control the size of the pellets used for nest construction, and indirectly also the porosity of nest walls.
claims.source: Recent studies have shown that termites can control the size of the pellets used for nest construction, and indirectly also the porosity of nest walls (Zachariah et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zachariah et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Substrate porosity plays an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest.
claims.source: In turn, substrate porosity is known to play an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest (Singh et al., 2019) and the moisture content of pellets can also affect the mechanical properties of the mound itself (Zachariah et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The moisture content of pellets can affect the mechanical properties of the mound.
claims.source: In turn, substrate porosity is known to play an important role for ventilation and drainage of the nest (Singh et al., 2019) and the moisture content of pellets can also affect the mechanical properties of the mound itself (Zachariah et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Zachariah et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The conclusions are relatively robust to changes in substrate porosity and moisture content.
claims.source: In relation to our own experiments, however, our scaling analyses (Appendix 3) indicate that our conclusions are relatively robust to changes in substrate porosity and moisture content.
claims.evidence: This is based on scaling analyses presented in Appendix 3.

claims.claim: Porosity only controls the time scale of water uptake from the reservoir by capillary rise.
claims.source: For example, porosity only controls the time scale of water uptake from the reservoir by capillary rise, which must be small enough to keep the clay disk hydrated, and this assumption remains valid up to mm-size pores in the new construction.
claims.evidence: This is based on scaling analysis in Appendix 3.

claims.claim: The addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography.
claims.source: Similarly, for local curvature, the addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography, and such additional 'roughness' can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at those locations.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the effect of pellet addition on surface roughness.

claims.claim: Additional roughness from pellet addition can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at locations of high convexity.
claims.source: Similarly, for local curvature, the addition of new pellets to regions of high convexity is likely to make the surface less smooth than the initial topography, and such additional 'roughness' can only increase the effect of focusing evaporation at those locations.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the effect of roughness on evaporation.

claims.claim: Calovi et al., 2019 pointed to an effect of surface curvature on termite construction behavior.
claims.source: Previous work by Calovi et al., 2019 had pointed to an effect of surface curvature on termite construction behavior.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Calovi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In Calovi et al., 2019, pellet depositions are attracted by convex features, while termite activity was concentrated at regions of maximum concavity.
claims.source: While our two studies emphasize the same point, we should note that our results and the results reported in Calovi et al., 2019 are not entirely consistent, because in our experiments, pellet depositions are attracted by convex features, while in Calovi et al., 2019 termite activity was concentrated at regions of maximum concavity.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the current study results and those reported in Calovi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The measure in Calovi et al., 2019 is a correlation between concavity and digging activity, not building.
claims.source: As this previous study did not distinguish digging from deposition activity, we believe that their measure is a correlation between concavity and digging activity, not building.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of results from Calovi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Concave regions should attract digging activity as predicted by the model.
claims.source: The fact that concave regions should attract digging activity is predicted by our model (see Materials and methods) and was visible also in our experiments where concavity (Figure 3D) attracted digging at the base of wall-like cues (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by model predictions and experimental observations shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Termites dig along the humidity gradient, that is toward the most humid region.
claims.source: Note that such behavior can be interpreted as termites digging along the humidity gradient, that is toward the most humid region.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed digging behavior.

claims.claim: In the absence of loose pellets, spontaneous digging usually started right above the hydration holes of the setup.
claims.source: Accordingly, in many preliminary experiments we observed that, in the absence of loose pellets, spontaneous digging usually started right above the hydration holes of our setup (Figure 3B) as a further confirmation of the termite ability to sense and respond to humidity gradients.
claims.evidence: This is supported by observations from preliminary experiments.

claims.claim: Termites would focus pellet depositions at regions of strong evaporation flux as a general mechanism capable of organizing termite building activity.
claims.source: In our study, we have outlined a general mechanism capable of organizing termite building activity: termites would focus pellet depositions at regions of strong evaporation flux.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on experimental and analytical results.

claims.claim: The building rule is embedded in the shape itself of the nest internal structure.
claims.source: In turn, evaporation flux co-varies with surface curvature, which implies that the building rule is embedded in the shape itself of the nest internal structure.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated relationship between curvature and evaporation.

claims.claim: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms.
claims.source: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms (see e.g. Grassé, 1984), which indicates that the nest-building process should also be different.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Grassé, 1984 and general knowledge.

claims.claim: The nest-building process should be different for different termite species.
claims.source: The nests built by termites of different genera or species show a large diversity of forms (see e.g. Grassé, 1984), which indicates that the nest-building process should also be different.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of nest forms.

claims.claim: The nest building behavior of termites must rely on more complex 'building rules' than the simple ones highlighted in this study.
claims.source: Arguably, the nest building behavior of termites, shaped by millions of years of evolution, must rely on more complex 'building rules' than the simple ones highlighted here.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the complexity of natural nest building.

claims.claim: The nests built by all termite species rely on a small number of architectural elements such as pillars and branching surfaces.
claims.source: Nonetheless, it is interesting to notice that the nests built by all species rely on a small number of architectural elements such as pillars and branching surfaces.
claims.evidence: This is based on general knowledge about termite nest architecture.

claims.claim: Simple variation of the basic building pattern coupled with variation of substrate evaporation would be sufficient to explain a large part of termite nest diversity.
claims.source: We can imagine that, perhaps, simple variation of the basic building pattern described here, coupled with variation of the substrate evaporation itself (e.g. under the effect of air currents, the properties of the building material, and heat produced by the colony itself) would still be sufficient to explain a large part of termite nest diversity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claims.claim: Ocko et al., 2019 showed that a single mechanism can be responsible for determining the overall shape of nests made by various species.

results.result: Pellet collection by termites was spatially homogeneous across the experimental arena, showing no preference for specific locations. Collections were distributed evenly over the clay disk and occurred in a relatively random fashion, compatible with a collection mechanism driven only by termite occupancy rather than local topography.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C29, C32, C62, and C63 are directly supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 2A and 2B. The homogeneous distribution of collections contrasts sharply with the concentrated deposition patterns, providing clear evidence that collection behavior is not topographically guided.

results.result: Pellet depositions were spatially concentrated at specific locations: the tips of pre-existing pillars and the edges of the clay disk. Termites targeted these specific regions when depositing pellets, indicating the presence of strong stimuli for deposition at these sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C30, C33, and C64 are well-supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and 3. The concentrated deposition patterns at pillar tips and disk edges are consistently observed across multiple experiments and clearly documented in the figures.

results.result: The conditional probability of deposition given termite occupancy was high at pillar tips and disk edges, while occupancy itself was high near pillars and walls but dropped at deposition sites. This indicates that these regions drive termite depositions rather than simply attracting termite aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34 and C65 are supported by experimental data in Figures 2D and 2E. The analysis of conditional probabilities P(D|O) and P(C|O) provides quantitative evidence that deposition sites are not merely areas of high termite presence, but locations with specific cues that trigger deposition behavior.

results.result: In experiments with wall-shaped topographic cues, pellet deposition focused at the wall tips (high curvature) rather than uniformly along the top edge (constant elevation) in 7 out of 11 experiments. This experimental design allowed disentangling the roles of elevation and curvature, pointing to curvature as the dominant cue for pellet deposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C37, C38, and C66 are supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1 and shown in Figure 3. The wall experiment design cleverly separates elevation from curvature effects. However, the result holds in only 7/11 experiments (64%), which suggests curvature is dominant but not the sole factor. The conclusion is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Experimental pellet depositions and computational simulations based solely on surface curvature showed fair qualitative agreement, with both concentrating in regions of highest convexity. This supports the hypothesis that surface curvature alone is sufficient to guide termite depositions, at least as a first approximation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 are supported by comparison of experimental data with simulation results shown in Figures 2C and 3. The qualitative agreement between experiments and curvature-only simulations provides evidence for the sufficiency of curvature as a cue. However, the authors appropriately note this is a 'first approximation' and 'qualitative' agreement, acknowledging limitations.

results.result: All pellet deposition regions correspond to local maxima in evaporation flux. Chemical garden experiments using salt deposition as an evaporation marker showed that salt deposits matched closely with regions of highest termite building activity, indicating that termite deposition probability covaries with evaporation flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C51, C52, and C53 are supported by chemical garden experiments shown in Figure 4C and D, combined with analytical calculations. The correspondence between salt deposition patterns (marking evaporation) and termite deposition patterns provides direct experimental evidence for the evaporation hypothesis. However, C51 contains speculative language ('propose') which is appropriate given the correlational nature of the evidence.

results.result: Evaporation flux is directly proportional to the local curvature of nest surfaces in the diffusive regime. This relationship was demonstrated analytically through mathematical derivation and confirmed experimentally through chemical garden experiments, establishing a close coupling between surface curvature and evaporation flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C48, and C68 are supported by mathematical proof in Appendix 2 and experimental validation in Figure 4. The analytical derivation provides theoretical foundation, while chemical garden experiments provide empirical confirmation. The proportionality relationship is well-established for the diffusive regime, though the authors appropriately note this applies specifically to conditions near the evaporating substrate.

results.result: Surface curvature is sufficient to organize termite building activity, with termites likely sensing curvature indirectly through substrate evaporation. This constitutes a general mechanism where termites focus pellet depositions at regions of strong evaporation flux, and the building rule is embedded in the shape of the nest structure itself through the covariation of evaporation flux with surface curvature.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C109, and C110 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the convergence of experimental observations (Figures 2-3), computational simulations (Figure 3), analytical derivations (Appendix 2), and chemical garden experiments (Figure 4). The use of 'likely' in C9 appropriately acknowledges that the sensory mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The evidence strongly supports curvature sufficiency and the evaporation-mediated mechanism.

results.result: The experimental setup maintained a stationary evaporation process, with the clay disk constantly humid and moisture evaporating while being replenished from below. Temperature and humidity measurements confirmed evaporation signatures: a net increase in humidity and decrease in temperature from outside to inside the clay disk, with both quantities remaining relatively stable indicating steady-state conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 describe the experimental conditions and are supported by direct measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The temperature and humidity data clearly show the expected signatures of evaporative cooling and humidity gradients. These measurements validate the assumption of steady-state evaporation that underlies the theoretical analysis.

results.result: Close to the evaporating substrate, humidity transport occurs by diffusion and is determined by the humidity gradient. Scaling arguments demonstrate that termites live in a viscous boundary layer where humidity transport is diffusive.
results.evaluation: Claims C46 and C47 are supported by citations to established physics literature (Langmuir 1918, Hisatake et al. 1993, Soar et al. 2019) and scaling arguments presented in Appendix 3. The diffusive regime assumption is critical for the theoretical analysis linking curvature to evaporation, and the authors provide appropriate justification through both literature and scaling analysis.

results.result: Curvature and evaporation are interchangeable stimuli everywhere except at the clay disk edge, where material transition creates a strong humidity gradient despite weak surface curvature. The disk edge appears nearly flat to a walking termite but represents a thin cusp of humid material with strong evaporation, analogous to coffee stain formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C60 are supported by computational analysis of humidity gradients (Figure 4) and analogy to well-established coffee stain physics (Deegan et al. 1997). This explains why depositions occur at disk edges despite low apparent curvature, reconciling the curvature hypothesis with edge deposition observations. The reasoning is sound and supported by both simulation and physical analogy.

results.result: Salt traces in chemical garden experiments were less pronounced on walls than pillars, consistent with weaker maximum humidity gradients in the wall case. This may explain the larger variability in termite construction patterns with wall cues, where depositions can start at wall tips or other top edge locations, with initial choices then reinforced by positive feedback mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C55, C57, C58, and C59 are supported by observations from chemical garden experiments (Figure 4C-D), computational simulations (Figure 4A-B), and experimental variability documented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2. The explanation linking weaker gradients to higher variability is logical and consistent with the data, though the causal connection is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: The findings reconcile previous discordant results pointing to either curvature or humidity as relevant stimuli by demonstrating their coupling. The apparent inconsistency with Calovi et al. 2019 (which found activity at concave regions) is explained by that study measuring digging rather than building activity, as concave regions should attract digging toward humid regions as predicted by the model and observed in the current experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C103-C106 provide important context by reconciling the current findings with previous literature. The reinterpretation of Calovi et al. 2019 as measuring digging rather than building is logical and supported by the authors' own observations of digging at concave regions (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). This reconciliation strengthens the overall narrative by explaining apparent contradictions in the literature.

results.result: The estimated humidity gradients in the experimental setup correspond to humidity variations of 10-100% across distances not larger than termite body length (millimeter scale). These variations must be sensed by termites, as they exceed the discrimination thresholds demonstrated for Coptotermes gestroi over much larger spatial scales in previous experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C84 and C85 are supported by calculations from estimated humidity gradients combined with termite body size, and comparison with previously reported sensory capabilities (Gautam and Henderson 2011). The scaling argument is sound: if termites can discriminate 75-98% humidity differences over centimeters, they should detect 10-100% differences over millimeters. This provides crucial support for the plausibility of humidity-based sensing.

results.result: The experiments do not support a role for cement pheromones in early deposition site selection. Construction occurred reliably on fresh clay and sterilized pellets without pheromone markings, simulations reproduced results without pheromones, and these findings agree with recent work by other authors. Pheromones are not necessary to explain early deposition patterns, though other roles are not ruled out.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 and C94 are supported by experimental design (using unmarked materials), simulation results (Figure 3), and agreement with cited literature (Fouquet et al. 2014, Petersen et al. 2015, Green et al. 2017). The conclusion is appropriately scoped to 'early deposition site selection' and acknowledges that pheromones might play other roles (C93). The evidence clearly demonstrates pheromones are not necessary for the observed patterns.

results.result: In the experiments, the building substrate was constantly moist. Under natural conditions where moisture may not constantly replenish, evaporation flux might be maintained by humidity in recently dropped pellets, making construction self-sustainable. However, it would be difficult to distinguish this scenario from one involving cement pheromones added to pellets, and pheromones may play roles in other aspects of building behavior such as aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 acknowledge limitations and speculate about natural conditions. C90 is a factual description of experimental conditions. C91-C93 are explicitly speculative (using 'suggest,' 'would be very hard,' 'do not rule out'). The speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified, but these claims about natural conditions and alternative mechanisms are not directly tested. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about generalization beyond their experimental conditions.

results.result: Termites are particularly sensitive to humidity due to their small size and soft cuticle. Coptotermes species can only survive in high-humidity environments and can discriminate humidity differences over centimeter scales. Recent studies show humidity affects nest building by triggering expansion events and affecting pellet collection and deposition. The current experiments confirm this trend and suggest moisture variations constitute a local blueprint for construction.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C79 establish the biological plausibility of humidity-based sensing through established knowledge (C71-C72) and cited experimental evidence (C73, C75-C78). The synthesis in C79 connecting previous work to current findings is well-supported. This background is essential for establishing that termites have the sensory capability to detect the humidity gradients proposed as construction cues.

results.result: The conclusions are relatively robust to changes in substrate porosity and moisture content based on scaling analyses. Porosity only controls the timescale of water uptake by capillary rise, which remains valid up to millimeter-size pores. Addition of pellets to convex regions likely increases surface roughness, which would only enhance evaporation focusing at those locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are supported by scaling analyses in Appendix 3 and logical inference about roughness effects. The robustness analysis is important for assessing generalizability. The arguments are sound: porosity affects dynamics but not steady-state patterns, and roughness would amplify rather than diminish the curvature-evaporation relationship. However, these are theoretical arguments rather than direct experimental tests.

results.result: Termites dig along humidity gradients toward the most humid regions. In preliminary experiments without loose pellets, spontaneous digging usually started right above the hydration holes of the setup, confirming termite ability to sense and respond to humidity gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C107 and C108 are supported by observations from preliminary experiments (Figure 3B) and model predictions. The observation that digging occurs at hydration holes (the most humid locations) provides direct evidence for humidity-directed digging behavior. This supports the broader hypothesis of humidity-guided behavior and helps explain the relationship between digging and building activities.

results.result: Termite nests show large diversity of forms across species, indicating different building processes. Natural nest building likely relies on more complex rules than those identified here. However, all species use similar architectural elements (pillars, branching surfaces), and simple variations of the basic building pattern coupled with substrate evaporation variations might explain much nest diversity, analogous to how Ocko et al. 2019 showed a single mechanism can determine overall mound shape across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are speculative discussions about generalizability to natural conditions and other species. C111 and C114 state established facts about nest diversity. C112, C113, and C115 are explicitly speculative ('indicates,' 'must rely,' 'we can imagine'). The speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified, but these claims about natural complexity and cross-species generalization are not directly tested. The analogy to Ocko et al. 2019 (C116) provides some support but is not definitive.

results.result: Beyond termite architecture, many biological structures at microscopic scales show convoluted structures via tip growth and branching. Their morphogenesis may rely on coupling between local curvature and growth-stimulating cues. While curvature can affect cell behavior through direct mechanical sensing, curvature guidance can also act indirectly by focusing gradients of diffusing growth-promoting quantities, as seen in mammalian lungs and jellyfish networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 place the findings in broader biological context. C117 and C119 state established knowledge about biological morphogenesis. C118 is speculative but reasonable extrapolation. C120 is supported by citations to analogous systems (Clément et al. 2012, Song et al. 2023). This discussion appropriately connects the termite findings to general principles of biological pattern formation, though the connections are suggestive rather than definitive.

results.result: The study used Coptotermes gestroi, a soil-nesting wood-feeding termite from South-East Asia that has spread globally. The species builds nests with scaffolds of interconnected pillars. Experiments used termites from captive colonies, with groups of 50 workers and 5 soldiers in controlled temperature and humidity conditions. The experimental setup consisted of a humid clay disk with topographic cues and pre-made pellets in a Petri dish with hydration system. A total of 16 pillar experiments, 11 wall experiments, and 6 no-cue experiments were conducted.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C135 describe the species, experimental subjects, conditions, and setup. These methodological details are well-documented with appropriate citations for species information (Li et al. 2010, Su et al. 2017, etc.) and clear descriptions of experimental protocols. The methods are sufficiently detailed for replication. Figure 1 and Table 1 support the experimental design descriptions.

results.result: Termites build complex nests through self-organization, with coordinated construction primarily mediated by stigmergic signals and cues embedded in nest structure. However, there is no scientific consensus about the nature of stimuli guiding construction and how termites sense them. Individual memory and proprioception are insufficient to explain nest construction, leading to the stigmergy concept first identified by Grassé.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C10-C13 provide established background knowledge about termite nest building and stigmergy, supported by foundational citations (Grassé 1959, Camazine et al. 2001, Bardunias and Su 2009a). These claims accurately represent the state of knowledge and set up the research question. The lack of consensus (C3) is supported by the review of conflicting literature in the introduction.

results.result: Previous research has proposed various stimuli for termite construction including pheromones, elevation, humidity gradients, and surface curvature. Evidence for cement pheromones is weak, though simulation studies assume their existence. Recent experimental studies indicate morphological and environmental features could guide construction, but digging and building activities often co-localize, preventing identification of specific cues. Computational models propose curvature-based mechanisms but lack empirical validation from direct behavioral observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C28 accurately review prior literature with appropriate citations (Bruinsma 1979, Khuong et al. 2011, Fouquet et al. 2014, Soar et al. 2019, Calovi et al. 2019, Ocko et al. 2019, Facchini et al. 2020, etc.). The review identifies key gaps: weak pheromone evidence, confounding of digging and building, and lack of empirical validation for models. This literature review appropriately motivates the current study's approach.

results.result: By providing loose unmarked pellets, the study prompted building without digging and quantified collections and depositions as separate actions. The alternative use of pillars and walls as topographic cues allowed disentangling the roles of elevation and curvature.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C66 describe key methodological innovations that address limitations of previous studies. The use of pre-made unmarked pellets eliminates pheromone confounds and separates collection from digging. The pillar vs. wall comparison cleverly separates elevation from curvature effects. These design choices are well-justified and effectively address the research questions.

results.result: Surface curvature is a powerful morphogenetic organizer that can drive formation of pillars, walls, and convoluted surfaces observed in termite nests. The relationship between curvature and evaporation was established a century ago by Langmuir (1918), who showed evaporation scales with mean curvature for water droplets.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C70 connect the findings to established principles. C67 is supported by citation to Facchini et al. 2020 and general knowledge of termite nest architecture. C70 cites foundational physics work (Langmuir 1918) establishing the curvature-evaporation relationship. These claims appropriately place the current work in historical and theoretical context.

results.result: Collective nest construction is dynamic, with pellet deposition constantly changing substrate shape and porosity, potentially affecting growth through feedback. Termites can control pellet size and nest wall porosity, which affects ventilation, drainage, and mechanical properties of the mound.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 acknowledge the dynamic nature of construction and cite relevant work on termite control of material properties (Zachariah et al. 2017, 2020, Singh et al. 2019). These claims appropriately recognize complexity beyond the current study's scope while noting that scaling analyses suggest robustness to these factors (C99-C102).

results.result: The authors demonstrate that termites show distinct spatial patterns in pellet collection versus deposition behavior. Pellet collection was distributed homogeneously across the experimental setup, while pellet deposition was concentrated at specific locations including the tips of topographic cues (pillars) and edges of the clay disk. This differential spatial targeting indicates that termites do not show preference for where they collect pellets but target specific regions when depositing.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states the study provides 'compelling' evidence for the claims, and the anonymous reviewer describes the experiments as 'ingenious' and notes the results are 'more than sufficient to justify their current claims.' The spatial separation of collection and deposition behaviors is central to the paper's argument and is not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: The authors establish a coupling between surface curvature and evaporation flux, demonstrating analytically and experimentally that evaporation flux is directly proportional to local surface curvature. Chemical garden experiments using saline solution showed that salt deposits (marking evaporation sites) matched closely with regions of highest termite building activity, supporting the hypothesis that evaporation flux explains deposition patterns.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer specifically praises the chemical garden experiment as 'a very ingenious low tech solution' to measuring evaporation patterns, noting it addresses what initially seemed like a missing experiment. The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling.' The reviewers accept the analytical and experimental demonstration of the curvature-evaporation relationship without critique.

results.result: The authors conclude that surface curvature is sufficient to organize termite building activity and that termites likely sense curvature indirectly through substrate evaporation. This represents the main mechanistic conclusion, supported by agreement between experimental results and curvature-based simulations, and the demonstrated relationship between curvature and evaporation.
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states this is the study's conclusion and describes the evidence as 'compelling.' The anonymous reviewer affirms that 'the work done so far is more than sufficient to justify their current claims' and describes the results as 'the best attempt on characterizing multiple cues that induce termite construction activity.' The mechanistic interpretation is accepted by both reviewers.

results.result: Using wall versus pillar topographic cues, the authors disentangled the roles of elevation and curvature in guiding deposition. In 7 out of 11 wall experiments, pellet deposition focused at wall tips (high curvature) rather than uniformly along the top edge (constant elevation), pointing to curvature rather than elevation as the dominant cue.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not question this experimental design or its interpretation. The anonymous reviewer notes the experiments were 'designed taking into account several different works' and that the results 'shine a light on how substrate evaporation is a sufficient descriptor of most of the results seen previously.' The experimental strategy to separate elevation from curvature is implicitly accepted.

results.result: Computational simulations based on curvature alone showed fair qualitative agreement with experimental deposition patterns, with both concentrating in regions of highest convexity. The simulations indicate that qualitatively similar construction results can be obtained without assuming a role for construction pheromone.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly notes that 'the authors have continued to use their expertise of numerical simulations and a previously developed model for termite construction, to highlight and verify their findings.' The simulation approach and its agreement with experiments is accepted without critique as supporting evidence.

results.result: The findings reconcile previous discordant results from different studies that pointed alternately to curvature or humidity as relevant stimuli. The authors address apparent inconsistency with Calovi et al. 2019 by suggesting that previous study measured digging (attracted to concavity) rather than building activity (attracted to convexity).
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states 'The findings reconcile discrepancies between previous studies' as a key contribution. The anonymous reviewer emphasizes this unification, noting the work 'possibly unifies the different hypothesis presented in the last 8 years into a single factor' and that results from different termite species 'are relatable and seem to be mostly consistent, improving the strength of the author's claims.'

results.result: The experiments do not support a role for cement pheromone in early deposition site selection. Construction occurred reliably on fresh clay and sterilized pellets with no pheromone markings, and the influence of cement pheromone can be excluded at least during early choice of deposition sites. However, the authors do not rule out possible roles for pheromones in other aspects like termite aggregation.
results.evaluation: The reviewers accept this conclusion without challenge. The anonymous reviewer notes the experiments used 'loose and unmarked pellets' and that this design successfully separated collection from deposition. The negative result regarding pheromones is implicitly accepted as part of the overall mechanistic framework that reviewers find compelling.

results.result: The authors establish biological plausibility by reviewing termite sensitivity to humidity. Coptotermes termites are particularly sensitive to humidity due to their physiology, can discriminate humidity differences over centimeter scales, and the calculated humidity gradients in the experiments (10-100% across termite body length) exceed known discrimination thresholds. Previous work showed moisture flux affects termite building activity.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not question the biological plausibility arguments or the humidity sensitivity of termites. The anonymous reviewer accepts that the mechanism is consistent with termite biology and notes the results are 'relatable' across different termite species, implicitly accepting the physiological reasoning.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that the experimental system is in steady-state evaporation with humidity transport occurring by diffusion. Measurements showed net humidity increase and temperature decrease from outside to inside the clay disk (evaporation footprint), with both quantities remaining stable over time. Scaling arguments confirm termites live in a viscous boundary layer where humidity transport is diffusive.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly notes that on first reading they felt 'the authors were missing an experiment: an array of humidity probes to measure evaporation' but then praises the alternative approach taken. The environmental characterization and steady-state assumptions are accepted without critique.

results.result: The experimental design innovation of providing loose, unmarked pellets allowed the authors to prompt building activity without digging and to quantify collections and depositions as separate actions, overcoming a key limitation of previous studies where digging and deposition came in pairs.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer implicitly praises this methodological innovation by noting the experiments were 'ingenious' and 'designed taking into account several different works.' The separation of collection from deposition is accepted as a key methodological advance that enables the main findings.

results.result: The authors speculate that similar curvature-evaporation coupling mechanisms may apply to other biological morphogenesis processes beyond termite nests, including tip growth and branching in mammalian lungs and jellyfish gastrovascular networks, where curvature guidance acts indirectly by focusing gradients of diffusing growth-promoting factors.
results.evaluation: The editor notes 'the authors do not discuss how their results affect our understanding of insect nest construction or animal-built structures more broadly,' indicating this broader context was initially insufficient. The anonymous reviewer acknowledges 'the authors have added more clarity into different biological systems in which these results could be applied' in revision, but suggests even more could be added about applications to swarm robotics. The broader implications remain somewhat underdeveloped.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C37, C38, C66 regarding curvature dominance over elevation. Both evaluations find the wall experiment design compelling and accept the conclusion that curvature is the dominant cue, though OpenEval notes the 64% success rate while peer reviewers accept the design without questioning this limitation.

Perfect agreement on claims C61, C66 regarding methodological innovations. Both evaluations praise the use of unmarked pellets and the experimental design separating collection from deposition. Peer reviewer explicitly calls the experiments 'ingenious' while OpenEval describes them as 'well-justified.'

Strong agreement on claims C71-C79 regarding biological plausibility of humidity sensing. Both evaluations accept the physiological evidence and sensory capabilities of termites. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of the supporting citations while peer reviewers implicitly accept this reasoning without critique.

Strong agreement on claims C69, C103-C105 regarding reconciliation with previous literature. Both evaluations explicitly praise this contribution. Editor states findings 'reconcile discrepancies between previous studies' and anonymous reviewer notes work 'possibly unifies the different hypothesis presented in the last 8 years.'

Strong agreement on claims C86, C87, C89, C94 regarding pheromone independence. Both evaluations accept that pheromones are not necessary for early deposition site selection. Peer reviewers note the use of 'loose and unmarked pellets' while OpenEval emphasizes the experimental design and simulation support.
